ten-frame.name: Ten Frame
ten-frame.metaTitle: Free Interactive Ten Frame Tool | LessonCraftStudio
ten-frame.metaDescription: A free online ten-frame for the classroom. Drag counters to build numbers, count, and explore early addition — no login, no install, works on any device.
about: A ten-frame is one of the most powerful pictures in early mathematics: ten boxes in two rows of five that let children see a number instead of only saying it. This free interactive ten-frame lets a child drag counters into the frame and watch each number take shape, one box at a time.

Because the frame always holds ten, children quickly begin to see numbers in relation to ten — that seven is "three away from full," or that five fills exactly one row. That sense of quantity is the foundation that counting, addition, subtraction, and place value all grow from.

It runs right in the browser on tablets, phones, and classroom computers, with nothing to install and no account to create. There is no timer and no score — just a calm, hands-on space to explore numbers.
howToUse: Display the ten-frame on a whiteboard or hand it to children on tablets, and ask them to show a number by dragging counters into the boxes.
Fill the top row first, then the bottom, so children build the habit of seeing ten as two fives.
Ask "how many more to make ten?" and let children add counters until the frame is full.
Use a double ten-frame to stretch the same thinking from ten up to twenty.
classroomIdeas: Flash a quantity for a few seconds, hide it, and ask children how many they saw — a quick way to build instant number recognition.
Show a number on the frame and ask children to say its partner to ten (a 4 needs 6 more).
Build two small numbers on a double frame and count the total together to introduce addition.
Let a child build any number they like and explain to a partner how they see it.

number-line.name: Number Line
number-line.tagline: Jump along to add and subtract
number-line.metaTitle: Free Interactive Number Line Tool | LessonCraftStudio
number-line.metaDescription: A free online number line for the classroom. Count, skip-count, and see addition and subtraction as jumps — no login, no install, works on any device.
about: A number line turns numbers into a journey: a straight path where every step has its place and bigger numbers live further along. This free interactive number line lets children count forward and back, take jumps, and see how numbers are spaced in order.

Seeing addition as jumps to the right and subtraction as jumps to the left gives children a mental model they can carry for years. It connects the act of counting to the size and order of numbers in a way that loose counters cannot.

It runs right in the browser on tablets, phones, and classroom computers, with nothing to install and no account to create. There is no timer and no score — just a calm space to explore how numbers move.
howToUse: Show the number line on a whiteboard and count along it together, pointing to each number as you say it.
Model addition by starting on a number and jumping forward, and subtraction by jumping back.
Practise skip-counting by twos, fives, and tens by taking equal jumps along the line.
Ask children to predict where a jump will land before they take it.
classroomIdeas: Give a start number and a number of jumps, and ask children where they will land.
Show a finished jump and ask children to describe the addition or subtraction it shows.
Use the line to compare two numbers — which is further along, and how far apart are they?
Let children invent their own jump story and act it out on the line.

ruler.name: Ruler
ruler.tagline: Measure length in cm and inches
ruler.metaDescription: A free online ruler for the classroom. Measure length in centimetres and inches and explore early measurement — no login, no install, works on any device.
about: Measuring is one of the first ways children connect numbers to the real world, and a ruler is where it begins. This free interactive ruler lets children measure length in centimetres and inches and see how a number describes how long something is.

Working with a ruler builds the careful habits early measurement depends on: lining up the start at zero, reading the marks in order, and naming the unit. These are the same habits children will later bring to rulers, tapes, and scales of every kind.

It runs right in the browser on tablets, phones, and classroom computers, with nothing to install and no account to create. There is no timer and no score — just a calm space to explore length and measurement.
howToUse: Show the ruler on a whiteboard and point out where measuring starts — at the zero mark, not the edge.
Measure a line together, reading the centimetres in order as you go.
Switch between centimetres and inches to show that the same length can be named in different units.
Compare two lengths and talk about which is longer and by how much.
classroomIdeas: Show a measured line and ask children to read its length before you reveal the answer.
Ask children to find something that is about a given length, then check it against the ruler.
Measure the same object in centimetres and inches and talk about why the numbers differ.
Order several lengths from shortest to longest and measure to check the order.

sound-boxes.name: Sound Boxes
sound-boxes.tagline: Push a chip for every sound you hear
sound-boxes.metaDescription: Free online Elkonin sound boxes for the classroom. Say a word, push a chip for each sound, then reveal the letters — no login, no install, on any device.
about: Sound boxes — often called Elkonin boxes — give children a way to see something invisible: the individual sounds inside a spoken word. A picture appears, the word is spoken aloud, and the child pushes one chip into a box for every sound they hear. Three boxes for "ship," four for "frog" — the boxes quietly confirm the answer without a single red X.

Segmenting words into phonemes is one of the strongest predictors of early reading success, and it comes straight out of the Science of Reading playbook: first hear the sounds, then map them to letters. That is exactly how this tool is built. Start with chips only for pure phonemic awareness, then tap the letters button and watch each sound's spelling appear in its box — the bridge from listening to reading, made visible.

It runs in the browser on whiteboards, tablets, and classroom computers, with nothing to install and no account to create. Word lists follow a phonics progression from simple three-sound words to blends and vowel teams, every word comes with a friendly picture and spoken audio, and there is no timer and no score — just a calm space to stretch words out, sound by sound.
howToUse: Pick a word list that matches your phonics focus — the starter list of simple three-sound words is a good first stop.
Tap the speaker to hear the word, then say it together slowly, stretching it out.
Have children push one chip into a box for each sound they hear, left to right, saying each sound as the chip lands.
Tap the letters button to reveal how each sound is spelled — one sound per box, even when the spelling is two letters like "sh."
Use the arrows to move to the next word, or open the word list to jump to any word your group needs.
classroomIdeas: Warm up whole-class on the whiteboard: say the word, have everyone tap an invisible box on their desk for each sound, then let one child push the chips up front.
At the small-group table, set the word filter to 2–3 sounds for children who are still building the skill, and 4–5 sounds for those ready to stretch.
Play "secret word": hide the picture, say a word yourself, and have children build the sounds before the reveal.
Type in this week's spelling or decodable words and use the same routine your class already knows — same boxes, your words.
Let a child at a center tap the speaker, push the chips, then check themselves by revealing the letters.

blending-board.name: Blending Board
blending-board.tagline: Flick the cards, blend the word
blending-board.metaTitle: Free Online Blending Board for Phonics | LessonCraftStudio
blending-board.metaDescription: Free blending board for phonics lessons. Flick letter cards to build words, sweep to blend, and let real words earn a picture — no login, on any device.
about: A blending board puts word-building in children’s hands: two or three columns of letter cards, and every flick of a column builds a new word to blend. Change just the first card and “sat” becomes “mat” becomes “pat” — the word chains that make successive blending click, without a box of laminated cards to shuffle and drop.

Blending is the other half of the phonemic-awareness pair: children segment words into sounds, then pull sounds back together into words. This board is built for that second half, the Science of Reading way. Sweep across the cards and each one lights up in order as the class blends aloud; then the word is spoken whole. Real words earn a picture, and made-up ones earn a friendly robot — because reading “zat” correctly is every bit as much a win as reading “sat,” and the robot says so without a single red X.

Decks follow a phonics progression, from a first handful of letters to digraphs and blends, in eleven languages. And because no class learns letters in the same order, you can build your own deck from just the cards your class has been taught — the board then only ever builds words your children can actually decode. It runs in the browser on whiteboards and tablets, with no login, no timer, and no score.
howToUse: Pick the deck that matches your phonics scope — the starter deck covers a first set of letters and sounds.
Flick a column, or tap the die for a surprise word, and give children a moment to read the cards.
Have the class blend the word aloud — then sweep across the blend bar so each card pulses in order and the word is spoken whole.
Watch for the badge: a picture means it is a real word, the robot means it is a made-up word that was still read correctly.
Change one card at a time to build a word chain — sat, mat, map, mop — so children hear how one sound changes the whole word.
classroomIdeas: Play “real or robot?”: build a word, have everyone blend it and vote before the sweep, then reveal the badge together.
Run a word chain warm-up: start from a word your class knows and change exactly one card each turn, reading every step aloud.
In the custom deck, switch off every card you have not taught yet — the board will only build words your group can decode, which makes it a safe reading centre.
Each Monday, add the week’s new letters or digraphs to your deck and let the class discover which new real words they unlock.
Pair it with Sound Boxes for the full routine: segment a word into its sounds there, then come back and blend words here.

letter-tiles.name: Letter Tiles
letter-tiles.tagline: An open magnetic board for building words
letter-tiles.metaTitle: Free Online Letter Tiles for Word Building | LessonCraftStudio
letter-tiles.metaDescription: Free magnetic letter tiles for phonics and spelling. Drag letters onto the board, hear anchor words, and check real words — no login, on any device.
about: Letter tiles are the classic word-building manipulative: a tray of magnetic letters and an open board where any word can take shape. This digital board keeps everything teachers love about the physical version — tiles that snap side by side, a tray that never runs out of letters — and adds the one thing plastic letters cannot do: every tile can talk. Tap a letter and it says its anchor word, so a child who has forgotten which letter makes a sound can find it again on their own.

The board is built for encoding — the spelling half of phonics. Children segment a word into sounds, then pick the letter for each sound and build it. When they press check, the board reads their word aloud. Real words earn a picture; a child’s own inventive spelling is simply read back, never marked wrong — because a kindergartner who writes “kat” has done real phonemic work, and a red X would undo it. There is no timer, no score, and nothing to get wrong on an open board.

A picture alphabet puts an anchor image on every tile, in the tradition of the German Anlauttabelle — and it works in all eleven languages, each with its own tray, its own anchor words, and its own high-frequency word list. Word cards from the Sound Boxes word bank turn the board into a guided spelling station: the child hears a word, builds it letter by letter, and optional ghost boxes show how many letter chunks it needs.
howToUse: Drag letters from the tray onto the board — they settle onto the writing lines and snap neatly next to their neighbours.
Tap any tile to hear its anchor word, the same way a child uses a picture alphabet chart.
Build a word, then press the check button: the board reads the letters left to right and speaks the word.
Watch for the badge: a picture means a real word. Anything else is simply read aloud — never marked wrong.
Open the word cards for a guided round: the child hears a word, builds it, and checks — with optional letter boxes as a scaffold.
classroomIdeas: Morning word work: put yesterday’s word family on the board and have children change one letter at a time — cat, hat, hot, hop.
Sound hunt: say a word aloud, have children find the letter for its first sound by tapping tiles and listening to the anchor words.
Invented-spelling journal warm-up: children build the word exactly as they hear it, the board reads it back, and the class compares it with the book spelling.
Name station: children build their own names and classmates’ names — the board reads every name aloud without judging it.
Guided spelling with word cards: deal a card, build the word in the ghost boxes, and let the picture badge confirm the match.

calendar-wall.name: Calendar Wall
calendar-wall.metaTitle: Free Interactive Calendar Wall for the Classroom | LessonCraftStudio
calendar-wall.metaDescription: Free interactive calendar for morning meeting: the spoken date, a days-in-school counter with bundling, and a weather graph — no login, on any device.
about: The calendar wall is the heart of the K-2 morning meeting: the date, the days we have been in school, and what the weather is doing outside. This digital wall replaces the laminated pockets and paper straws with one screen the whole class can see — and every element is touchable, because in a good calendar routine it is a child, the calendar helper, who does the touching.

The mathematics is real, not decorative. Today’s card sits face-down until the helper flips it, and the date is spoken in real words — “Thursday, July sixteenth,” never a robotic digit reading. The days-in-school counter shows the same number three ways at once: straw bundles, a ten-frame, and the numeral. When day ten arrives, the class watches ten loose straws become one bundle — place value happening in front of them, and the hundredth day gets the same treatment with bunting. One tap moves all three representations together, something a physical wall can never do.

The weather graph turns the daily observation into the class’s first data work: one tap a day, one icon on the chart, and by mid-month there is a real pictograph to discuss — which weather has the most days, how many more sunny than rainy. Everything works in eleven languages with the date read the way each language actually says it, the week starting on the right day, and the whole routine ready the moment the projector turns on.
howToUse: Open the wall on your projector or whiteboard — the calendar shows the month with today’s card face-down.
Let the calendar helper flip today’s card: the date is spoken aloud in real words, and the class echoes it.
Move to Days in School and let the helper tap +1 — the straws, the ten-frame, and the number all move together.
Ask the class what the weather is doing, agree on one word, and let the helper tap it — the month’s graph grows by one.
Use the talk prompt under the graph for one minute of real data talk, and you are done — the whole routine in about ten minutes.
classroomIdeas: Yesterday–today–tomorrow chorus: read the three sentence strips together every morning — gold for multilingual learners.
Prediction before the flip: have the class say tomorrow’s day and date aloud today, then check with tomorrow’s flip.
Decade-day countdowns: three days before day 40, ask “what will the bundles look like?” and let the class draw their prediction.
Data detective: each Friday, ask one child to report the weather graph — how many of each, which is winning, how many days recorded in all.
The hundredth day: count to 100 by tens together as the ten bundles become one hundred — then keep counting past it (day 101 is a number too).

number-talk-easel.name: Number Talk Easel
number-talk-easel.tagline: Flash a picture, talk about the math
number-talk-easel.metaTitle: Free Number Talk & Subitizing Easel | LessonCraftStudio
number-talk-easel.metaDescription: Free quick-image easel for number talks: flash dots, frames or a bead rack for three seconds, then talk about how children saw it — no login needed.
about: A number talk starts with a picture you can only look at for a moment. This easel flashes a quantity image — scattered dots, dice patterns, ten frames, a bead rack, or seven ducks — for about three seconds, long enough to see structure and too short to count one by one. That constraint is the entire pedagogy: children stop counting and start seeing groups, and the roller-shade curtain that hides and reveals the picture is yours to control, including press-and-hold for exactly as long as your thumb is down.

What follows the flash matters more than the flash: children describe how they saw it, and every way of seeing is welcome. The easel never says right or wrong — there are no chimes, no stars, and the number itself stays hidden until you tap Count it, which counts the structure aloud and raises the answer card. In the discussion, a tap colors the dots the way a child grouped them — five red and three blue — and a crayon circles the pairs and fives children found.

The strings library is a year of number talks with zero preparation: sequences of three to five related images where each is a small variation of the last — five and some more, doubles, make ten — each with a one-line teaching note, flashing identically in every classroom. Build your own sets for the week, and run the whole routine in any of eleven languages, with the number words spoken the way your class says them.
howToUse: Pick a picture type and range — or start with today’s quick image, ready when the projector turns on.
Tap Show for a three-second flash, or press and hold to keep the picture up exactly as long as you want.
Ask: how many did you see? How did you see it? Collect every answer without judging any.
Tap Show again for a second look — the picture is identical — then Reveal to leave it open for the discussion.
Color the groupings children describe, circle structures with the crayon, and finish with Count it: the number is spoken and confirmed by counting the structure.
classroomIdeas: Daily warm-up: one quick image before math — three minutes, whole class, zero prep.
Same number, different look: flash 6 as dice, then a circle, then a ten frame — watch children discover the number stays the same.
Turn and talk: after the first flash, partners compare what they saw before the second look.
Strategy collection: tint one child’s grouping in color, then ask who saw it differently and tint that too — three decompositions of the same eight.
Make-ten talks: flash 9 + 3 on the double frame and ask how many the first frame still needs — the empty cells teach the strategy.

rekenrek.name: Rekenrek
rekenrek.tagline: Twenty beads, one push — see the number
rekenrek.metaTitle: Free Online Rekenrek — Number Rack | LessonCraftStudio
rekenrek.metaDescription: Free projectable rekenrek: slide five-red-five-white beads in one push, flash a quantity behind the curtain, hear the number spoken — up to a 100-bead wall.
about: A rekenrek looks like an abacus but teaches the opposite habit: instead of counting beads one by one, children learn to see numbers in chunks. Every rod carries five red beads and five white ones, so seven pushed to the left is visibly five-and-two — no counting required. This projectable rekenrek keeps that structure honest: beads slide in chains with a wooden clack, and showing a number in one push — grabbing the seventh bead and sweeping once — is the whole game. There are no timers, no scores, and no numeral on screen unless you ask for one, because the real instrument has none either.

The flash routine turns the rack into a number talk. Set the beads while the class watches, pull down the curtain, and flash the rack for two, three or five seconds — long enough to see five-and-two, too short to count one at a time. Children say what they saw and how they saw it, a volunteer rebuilds it in one push, and Reveal settles it — with the number word spoken aloud the way your class says it, in any of eleven languages. The half-curtain hides just the bottom row for the classic "how many are hiding?" missing-part game.

A library of ready bead sequences walks the year: one push, flash and rebuild, five and some more, doubles and near doubles, friends of ten, make ten to add, and the hundred wall — each step one small variation of the last, each with a one-line teaching note. Save your own sequences for the week, grow the rack from one rod to a ten-rack 100-bead wall, and let the Speak button say forty-seven while the class sees four full rows and seven — the number word and the structure landing together.
howToUse: Slide beads with a finger or the mouse — grab the seventh bead and sweep once to show 7 in one push; the beads travel as a chain with a clack.
Tap Say the number any time to hear the total spoken as a real number word — the numeral stays hidden unless you switch it on.
For a flash routine, set the beads, tap Cover, then Show for a timed flash — or press and hold to keep the rack visible exactly as long as your thumb is down.
Ask how many they saw and how they saw it, let a child rebuild the number in one push, then Reveal to settle it together.
Open the bead sequences for ready-made routines with teaching notes, or add racks — up to the 100-bead wall — for tens-and-ones work.
classroomIdeas: One-push warm-up: call a number to 10; a child shows it in a single sweep while the class checks — five-and-two, not seven ones.
Flash and rebuild: three seconds behind the curtain, partners agree on what they saw, one rebuilds it — the answer is a gesture, not a word.
How many are hiding? Show the total, drop the half-curtain over the bottom row, and let children reason from the part they can see.
Doubles and near doubles: build 4 and 4 on two rows, then push one more bead — children see how 4+5 leans on the double.
The hundred wall: on ten racks, build 47 as four full rows and seven — then say it aloud and hear how the number word matches the rows.

class-timer.name: Class Timer
class-timer.tagline: A calm picture of the time you have left
class-timer.metaTitle: Free Visual Classroom Timer — No Alarm | LessonCraftStudio
class-timer.metaDescription: A calm visual timer for classroom transitions: a shrinking clock wedge, gentle voice cues and a warm chime instead of an alarm — free, no login.
about: Five minutes of cleanup goes better when the whole class can see the five minutes. This timer turns time into a picture — a coral wedge that quietly shrinks on a clock face, a jar filling with sand, a candle burning down, or a balloon drifting to a soft landing. There are no flashing colors, no ticking, no acceleration, and no alarm at the end: the time you have left is simply an amount children can glance at, the way they glance at the classic red-disc timer on your shelf. It times the routine — never a child.

The routine is one tap. Pick the minutes, pick what you are doing — Cleanup, Centers, Quiet reading, Pack-up, Turn and talk — and tap Start. A warm voice can announce the start in your classroom's language, whisper "one more minute" near the end, and finish with a gentle three-note chime and "time to gather." Need more time? The +1 minute button visibly grows the wedge back — the honest version of "I'm giving you one more minute" — and pausing dims the picture instead of hiding anything.

Saved timers make it a daily habit: your own one-tap presets keep the label, the minutes and the picture together, so "Cleanup 5:00 with the candle" is a single touch during a live transition. The corner view shrinks the timer to a small card you can snap beside another projected tool, and the minutes readout stays off by default — teachers can switch it on, but the picture is the point. The timer keeps perfect time even if the projector tab sleeps, and picks up exactly where it was if the page reloads.
howToUse: Tap a minutes chip — 1 to 30 — or nudge with +1/−1, then pick what you are doing so the label shows above the picture.
Tap Start. The wedge, sand, candle or balloon begins its slow, calm drain — continuous, never ticking.
While it runs you have exactly three controls: Pause, +1 min (the wedge visibly grows back), and End now.
Listen for the gentle cues: an optional halfway chime, a one-minute chime, and the warm three-note finish — never an alarm.
Save your favorite routines as one-tap presets, and use the corner view to run the timer beside another projected tool.
classroomIdeas: Cleanup with the wedge: "when the orange is gone, we sit on the carpet" — children read the remaining wedge from anywhere in the room.
Quiet reading with the candle: the slow burn sets a hushed mood, and the one-minute chime gives bookmarks time to go in.
Centers with saved presets: one tap starts the same 15 minutes every day, and +1 min honestly extends the round when the work is good.
Turn and talk in two minutes: the balloon drifts down while partners share — when it lands, eyes back on the teacher.
Beside the rekenrek: shrink the timer into the corner view and project a math tool next to it during warm-up routines.

name-sticks.name: Name Sticks
name-sticks.tagline: The fair jar — every name gets a turn
name-sticks.metaTitle: Free Random Name Picker — Name Sticks | LessonCraftStudio
name-sticks.metaDescription: A fair name-stick jar for the classroom: pull a stick, hear the name spoken, and pulled sticks rest in a visible cup until everyone has had a turn.
about: Every classroom has a jar of popsicle sticks — and every class has figured out how it gets gamed: the thumb that feels for a favorite stick, the quiet put-back, the cup that empties early so the same kids keep getting called. Name Sticks is the version that cannot cheat, and the class can see it. Every name goes in the jar as an illustrated stick, a pull is truly random, and pulled sticks rest in a visible cup until the jar is empty. When someone needs to go back in, the stick returns on the projector — in front of everyone.

A pull is one calm second: a wooden rattle, the stick rises, and the name presents big enough to read from the back — spoken aloud in your classroom's language if you like. Every name gets a small "say it like…" field, so Nguyễn, Aoife and Xiomara are pronounced right every single time — a child who hears their name mangled daily stops feeling the jar belongs to them. Skip returns a stick without burning the turn, and Absent lays a stick flat in its own tray until tomorrow.

The team maker shakes the whole jar into two to six animal-team cups — near-equal sizes with the extra spots landing randomly, never a last-kid-left-over moment — and you drag any stick between cups when two friends need distance. Class lists paste in one name per line and stay only on this device: names are never sent anywhere. Saved classes keep the cup's memory overnight, so Tuesday's fairness carries into Wednesday morning.
howToUse: Paste your class list — one name per line — and the sticks pour into the jar with their own little animal icons.
Tap the jar or Pull a stick: a short rattle, the stick rises, and the name shows big (and spoken, if you keep the voice on).
Pulled sticks rest in the cup for everyone to see; Skip puts a stick back without using up the turn, Absent parks it in the tray for today.
When the jar empties, the class sees "Everyone has had a turn" — tip the sticks back in and the cycle starts fresh.
Switch to Teams to shake the class into 2–6 animal-team cups, then drag any stick between cups to fine-tune.
classroomIdeas: Morning helper: one pull picks today's line leader — the cup proves to everyone that turns are truly fair across the week.
Turn and talk: set the pull to 2 and draw partner pairs — both sticks go to the cup, so pairings rotate through the whole class.
Center rotations: shake into four animal teams on Monday and keep the same teams all week — the grouping stays saved.
New-name week: use the "say it like…" field with the class — children love teaching the jar to say their name exactly right.
Fairness talk: let the class watch the cup fill and predict how many pulls until the jar is empty — turn-taking becomes math.

center-board.name: Center Board
center-board.tagline: Your rotation chart, running itself calmly
center-board.metaTitle: Free Center Rotation Board for K-3 | LessonCraftStudio
center-board.metaDescription: A projector rotation board for classroom centers: animal team cards slide station to station with a chime, a calm round timer, and QR links per station.
about: Centers run on one question asked thirty times an hour: "where do I go?" Center Board answers it from the projector. Stations sit as big illustrated cards — Listening, Math Table, Teacher Time — and every team's animal card is docked right under its station. When you tap Rotate, the cards physically slide one station over with a warm chime and a spoken "time to rotate," so a five-year-old watches their fox walk to the writing table. No spreadsheet grid, no legend to decode: it works like the pocket chart on your wall, but it moves.

The round timer is the calm kind: a small coral wedge empties beside the Rotate button, whispers "one minute — clean-up time" near the end, and then simply makes the button glow. It never rotates the room on its own — you might be mid-sentence with your guided-reading group, so the transition always waits for your tap. A substitute can run the whole block from the board alone: "Round 2 of 4" sits above the stations, and each station can carry a one-line note like "listen to the story, then draw your favorite part."

The board plugs into your other tools: pull today's teams straight from Name Sticks with one tap — same animals, same colors, kids' names on the cards — and give any station a LessonCraftStudio link, so the tablet basket at the listening center opens exactly the activity you chose, by QR card or a copied link. Drag any team card between stations when two friends need distance; the rotation keeps working around your change. Boards save per class, and each morning starts fresh at round one with your setup intact.
howToUse: Set up your stations — pick from twelve illustrated center icons, rename them your way, and add an optional note or voice-level badge.
Bring in your teams: import today's groups from Name Sticks or add animal teams right on the board.
Start the round timer (5–20 minutes). The wedge empties calmly; at one minute the clean-up cue plays.
When the Rotate button glows, finish your sentence, then tap it — the cards slide one station over with a chime.
Give a station a LessonCraft link and print its QR card so the tablet station opens exactly what you planned.
classroomIdeas: Daily 5 rotations: literacy stations with the teacher table as one stop — you see your striving readers while the board runs the room.
The substitute plan: save the board, leave "Round 2 of 4" on screen, and the note on each station card says what to do there.
Tablet listening center: tape the printed QR card to the table — kids scan and land exactly on this week's listening activity.
Uneven weeks: three teams on five stations just means two stations rest each round — every team still visits everything.
Fair transitions: kids watch their own animal card travel, so "where do I go?" answers itself without a single reminder.

learning-clock.name: Learning Clock
learning-clock.tagline: The clock that says the time the way people really say it
learning-clock.metaTitle: Free Interactive Learning Clock — Telling Time K-3
learning-clock.metaDescription: A big geared teaching clock for the projector: drag the hands and it says the time out loud — "half past 2" — with an arc that shows why. Free, no signup.
about: The Learning Clock is a big, friendly analog clock with real gearing: drag the minute hand all the way around and the hour hand creeps forward with it, exactly like the classroom clock on your wall. That one detail quietly fixes the most stubborn time-telling misconception — at 2:50, is it 2 o'clock or 3? Children who only ever see clocks drawn with the hour hand parked on a number never get to wrestle with that; here the answer is visible in the hands themselves.

The speech bubble is the part your class will remember. Set the clock to 2:30 and it doesn't recite "two thirty" — it says "half past 2", out loud, the way people actually say it. A tap on the little question mark draws a soft arc on the face showing exactly which half the words are talking about, and the numeral the phrase points to gives a friendly wave. Reading a clock and saying the time are two different skills; this tool teaches them together.

A five-stop difficulty ladder walks the whole journey: whole hours for the youngest, then half hours, quarters, five minutes, and finally to-the-minute times, where the bubble switches to the formal reading a station announcer would use. Task mode asks children to set the clock themselves, elapsed mode shades the time between a start and an end flag, and you can save your own class times — lunch, story time, home time — as prompts. It runs in the browser, no account needed.
howToUse: Project the clock and drag either hand — the bubble reads the new time aloud when you let go. Let children take turns being the one who sets it.
Pick the difficulty stop that matches your unit: whole hours, half hours, quarters, five minutes, or to the minute.
Tap the question mark when a phrase like "half past 2" needs unpacking — the arc shows exactly the stretch of clock the words describe.
Switch to Task mode and the clock asks for a time; children drag the hands and check. Misses get a gentle nudge, never a buzzer.
Use Elapsed mode for "how long until lunch?" — pin the start and end flags and the shaded arc shows the answer in hour-sized chunks.
classroomIdeas: Morning meeting: one child sets today's special time — the class reads it together before the bubble confirms it out loud.
Save your real class times — recess, library, home time — and use them as task prompts; children practice on times that matter to them.
The daily-schedule link: set the clock to the next transition and leave it on the projector; the hands and the wall clock will agree when it's time.
Quarter-hour scavenger hunt: call out "quarter to 4" and pairs race to set their own clock on tablets, then check against the board.
Elapsed-time stories: "We started reading at half past 9 and stopped at 10 past 10 — how long did we read?" Pin both flags and count the shaded chunks together.

place-value-lab.name: Place Value Lab
place-value-lab.tagline: Blocks, digits, and the number word — linked live
place-value-lab.metaTitle: Free Interactive Base-10 Blocks — Place Value Lab K-2
place-value-lab.metaDescription: A projector base-10 workmat: ten ones snap into a ten, and the number word lights up to show which part means tens and which means ones. Free, no signup.
about: The Place Value Lab is a base-10 blocks workmat with a twist no physical set can offer: three displays stay linked while you work. Tap blocks onto the mat and the numeral builds itself in labeled place columns — and beneath it, the number word assembles too, with its tens part and ones part glowing in the same colors as the columns. Twenty-four shows twenty in teal and four in coral; the connection between what we SAY and what we WRITE stops being invisible.

The bundling moment is the heart of place value, so the Lab makes it a moment worth watching. Collect ten loose ones and the mat offers a bundle — one tap, and the cubes squeeze together with a rubber-band snap and become a ten rod that slides into the tens column. It works the other way too: break a ten back into ten ones with a pop. That unbundling IS borrowing, and the premium Subtract lab stages it: take 17 from 42, hit the wall at two loose ones, and the borrow becomes something children physically do rather than a rule they memorize.

A Show me mode turns it into a gentle challenge — build the number you see, or the trickier version: build the number you HEAR. When a child hears the word and builds the digits reversed, the tool never buzzes; it names what they actually built, lights up the word parts, and invites another look. Premium adds the hundreds place and lets you save your class's own numbers — days of school, kids in the room — the numbers children actually care about. Free in the browser, no account needed.
howToUse: Project the mat and tap the + buttons to add blocks — the numeral and the number word build along with you.
Collect ten ones and tap the glowing bundle button: the snap into a ten rod is the place-value lesson in one second.
Tap any digit to interrogate it — its part of the word and its blocks flash together, and it is spoken alone.
Switch to Show me for build-what-you-hear challenges; misses get a warm comparison, never a buzzer.
In the Subtract lab (premium), watch borrowing become physical: break a ten, remove the marked blocks, done.
classroomIdeas: The daily number ritual: build the day-of-school count every morning and save it — the hundred-day party builds itself.
Zahlendreher clinic: say a tricky number aloud, let children build it, then tap the digits to see which part of the word said what.
Estimation warm-up: show a pile of ones, ask "can we make a ten?", and let a child perform the bundle for the class.
Partner check: one child types a number on the keypad, the other reads the word aloud before the speech button confirms it.
Borrowing theater: run one subtraction on the projector before workbook time — the pop of the breaking ten is the anchor image for the whole lesson.

picture-word-wall.name: Picture Word Wall
picture-word-wall.metaTitle: Free Picture Word Wall — 1,495 Illustrated Words K-3
picture-word-wall.metaDescription: A projector word wall of 1,495 illustrated nouns across 50 themes. Tap a card: it grows big and says its word out loud. Free, no signup, 11 languages.
about: The Picture Word Wall turns a shelf of vocabulary flashcards into something a wall of butcher paper never could be: a browsable, speaking wall of 1,495 illustrated nouns across 50 themes — animals, the kitchen, the beach, occupations, weather. Tap any card and it lifts out of the wall, grows large, and says its word out loud in a clear voice a child can replay as many times as she likes. The pictures are the same warm illustrations used across the whole platform, so a word learned here is recognised everywhere else.

The part no other word wall can do is the toggle. Every card holds both its singular and its plural, hand-checked rather than guessed, so one duck becomes three ducks and the word changes with the picture — and where the word does NOT change, the card says so out loud instead of pretending. In the languages that have grammatical gender, every card is colour-coded by its article and the article is always spoken with the noun, never apart from it, because that is how the word actually lives in a sentence.

Whisper mode is the quiet favourite: a word is spoken, the child finds its card, and a firefly drifts across the wall and lands on it. There is no timer, no score, and no wrong-answer sound — a miss just brings the firefly closer and says the word again, a little slower, so every round ends in success. Teachers can pin cards from any theme into their own named wall for the week and run a sixty-second read-through with the class each morning.
howToUse: Open a theme and project the wall — the cards are big enough to read from the back row.
Tap any card: it grows large and says its word out loud, with its article.
Use the one/many toggle to multiply the picture and hear the plural change with it.
Turn on Whisper mode and let children take turns finding the word they hear — the firefly lands when they do.
Long-press cards from any themes to pin your own wall, name it for the week, and read it together every morning.
classroomIdeas: Morning read-through: pin this week's eight words, name the wall, and chorally read it in sixty seconds each day.
Newcomer corner: a child with no shared language taps pictures and hears the word whole, article attached, as often as she likes — no writing, no speaking, no waiting.
Article sort: in a gender language, ask children to find every card of one colour on the wall before you say the word.
One and many: build a plural lesson entirely from the toggle — the picture proves the rule before the rule is named.
Theme preview: open the theme of your next unit and let the class name what they already know before you teach a single word.

hush-owl.name: Hush Owl
hush-owl.tagline: Let the owl sleep — a calm picture of the room’s voices
hush-owl.metaTitle: Hush Owl — A Calm Classroom Noise Meter for K-3
hush-owl.metaDescription: A sleepy owl dozes while your class keeps today’s voice level, and sustained loudness gently wakes him. No sirens, no red zones, no numbers — sound never leaves the device.
about: Hush Owl gives your classroom a shared, gentle picture of its own volume. A sleepy owl dozes on a branch on the projector; the room’s sound sways the branch, and only sustained loudness slowly wakes him — first his ear tufts twitch, then one sleepy half-blink, then he looks curiously around the room. A dropped pencil, a laugh, a chair scrape can never wake him. The class’s shared goal is simple and kind: let the owl sleep.

There are no sirens here, no red zones, no loudness numbers, no meters and no names — the feedback is about the room, never about a child. The owl is never angry; when it gets loud he simply wakes up curious, and about fifteen seconds of settled voices earn his contented sigh and return to sleep. A small wooden sign on the branch shows today’s target — Silent, Whisper voices, Partner voices, or Group-work voices — so children can always see the goal they are working toward together.

Hush Owl is built for privacy-conscious classrooms: the owl only listens right here in your room. Sound levels are measured on this device and nothing is ever recorded, saved, or sent anywhere. On school devices where the microphone is blocked, Teacher’s ears mode keeps everything working — you tap how the room sounds, and the owl responds just the same. Premium adds the voice-level choices, a sleepy cat and a little dragon, and a corner view that sits beside another projected tool.
howToUse: Open Hush Owl on the projector so the whole class can see the sleeping owl.
Pick today’s voices — the wooden sign on the branch shows the class the target.
Tap Start listening and allow the microphone when your browser asks.
Teach the goal once: our job is to let the owl sleep. The swaying branch shows the room’s sound right now.
If the room wakes him, just settle back down together — about fifteen seconds of calm voices and he falls asleep again.
classroomIdeas: Silent reading: set the sign to Silent and let the owl be the only reminder anyone needs.
Partner work: set Partner voices and let pairs self-check against the swaying branch instead of waiting for a shush.
Class meeting on day one: let the class discover what wakes the owl and agree together on how to help him sleep.
No microphone allowed at your school? Run Teacher’s ears mode and tap how the room sounds — the ritual works the same.
Corner view (Premium): keep a small owl beside your math tool during centers so the calm picture never leaves the wall.

wodb.name: Which One Doesn’t Belong?
wodb.tagline: Four things — and every answer can be right
wodb.metaTitle: Which One Doesn’t Belong? — K-3 Math Talk Grids
wodb.metaDescription: The beloved no-wrong-answer reasoning routine on your projector: 21 curated 2×2 grids of numbers, shapes, clocks and pictures where every answer is defensible. Free weekly grid.
about: Which One Doesn’t Belong? turns the beloved math-talk routine into a living projector tool. Four things appear in a 2×2 grid — numbers, shapes, dot patterns, clock faces, or illustrated pictures — and the class puzzles over which one doesn’t belong. The trick that makes children love it: every one of the four is a defensible answer, because each is the only one with some property. There is no wrong choice, only noticing.

A child taps their pick and it gently lifts — chosen for discussion, never marked correct — and up to all four can be lifted at once while four children defend four different corners. The speaker button offers sentence stems for emerging speakers, spoken aloud in your language. When the talk winds down, you reveal the four reasons cards one by one, each honoring somebody’s argument, and the grid glows warmly: every one was a good answer. No scores, no timers, no shame — ever.

A new featured grid arrives every week, free and complete. Premium opens the full curated library — 21 grids across ages 4 to 9, from counting dots to clock faces — plus the builder: assemble your own grid from 1,495 illustrated pictures, numbers, shapes, dots and clocks in about thirty seconds, add optional reasons, and save it for your class.
howToUse: Open the tool on the projector — this week’s featured grid is ready to play.
Ask the question: which one doesn’t belong? Give everyone quiet thinking time first.
Tap the choices children defend — each lifts gently, and several can be lifted at once.
Tap the speaker on a lifted card for a sentence stem when a child needs a starting frame.
When the talk is rich, tap Show the reasons and reveal each card — every child was right.
classroomIdeas: Morning meeting warm-up: one grid, five minutes, every hand up — because every answer works.
Turn-and-talk first: partners agree on a pick and a because-sentence before anyone taps.
Language practice: require the sentence stem frame aloud — it is the same frame the reasons cards use.
Build a grid about your current topic (Premium): four pictures from the theme you are teaching this week.
Let a child be the revealer: they tap each reasons card and read it to the class.

story-line.name: Story Line
story-line.tagline: Peg the story cards in order — then play your story
story-line.metaTitle: Story Line — Sequencing & Retelling Cards for K-2
story-line.metaDescription: A clothesline of illustrated story cards on your projector: children peg the beats in order, every peg is narrated with real sequence words, and a warm spotlight replays the whole tale. Two sets free.
about: Story Line turns the paper story map into a living clothesline. Fifteen illustrated card sets — everyday routines, nature cycles like the butterfly and the little seed, and shared tales like the enormous turnip — wait in a shuffled tray below the line. A child drags a card up and pegs it in place, and the narrator tells that beat with a real sequence word: First, the snowflakes fall all night long. Then, we build a round, happy snowman.

The gentle secret is that every pegged order plays. Sequence words belong to the positions, not the cards, so a jumbled line makes the story sound wonderfully wrong — and hearing At the end before the snow has even fallen is the kindest self-correction there is. The narrator never judges an order; there is no red X and no correct-order banner, only the little book button that offers the book’s way as another version, without ever moving a child’s cards.

Retell mode turns the narrator off: pegs make a single soft chime, and Play my story becomes a silent spotlight the child fills with their own voice — a genuine one-to-one oral-language moment. Nothing is recorded, saved, or scored, deliberately: the teacher listens, and that is the whole point. Premium opens all fifteen sets, retell mode, and teacher tray staging; Rain and Rainbow and Baking Day are free forever.
howToUse: Open Story Line on the projector — a free story set is dealt into the tray, shuffled.
Ask: what happens first? Drag that card up to the line and peg it — the narrator tells the beat.
Keep pegging. If the order comes out jumbled, just play it — the class will hear it and fix it.
Tap Play my story for the spotlight replay, auto-paced or tap-to-advance.
For retelling, switch the narrator off (Premium) and let your storyteller voice each beat as the spotlight moves.
classroomIdeas: Morning circle: one three-card set, three volunteers, one peg each — then play the class’s story.
Deliberately peg a story backwards and play it — the giggles teach the sequence words better than any drill.
Science talk: the butterfly and little-seed sets pair perfectly with your life-cycle unit.
Retell assessment moment: hide the narrator and listen while one child tells the whole line (nothing is recorded — just listen).
Language support: the sequence-word chips stay visible, so emerging speakers always have their next connective in view.

fraction-kitchen.name: Fraction Kitchen
fraction-kitchen.tagline: Cut real food into equal parts — and share it fairly
fraction-kitchen.metaTitle: Fraction Kitchen — Cut & Share Fractions Tool for Grades 2-3
fraction-kitchen.metaDescription: Children drag a knife to really cut a pizza, chocolate bar, or cake into halves, thirds, and fourths, share the slices fairly, and prove that two fourths fill one half. Free to start.
about: Fraction Kitchen brings the classic paper-folding fractions lesson to life as a warm, cheerful kitchen. A pizza, a chocolate bar, or a sheet cake sits on the cutting board, and faint guide lines show where a knife could travel. A child drags the friendly rounded knife along a line and the food really cuts, with a satisfying slice sound and the fraction spoken aloud in words: halves, thirds, fourths, sixths, eighths. There is no symbolic notation anywhere — this tool builds the meaning that ½ and ¾ will later attach to.

Not every guide line makes equal parts — and that is the whole lesson. Cut along an off-center line and the pieces simply come apart, sit visibly unequal for a moment, seesaw gently, and heal back together. It is physics, never a verdict: no red flash, no buzzer, no 'wrong'. A kind voice observes — once — that the pieces are not the same size, and the child looks for the cut that makes equal pieces. Slices then share out onto friends' plates for fair-share reasoning, and leftovers become discussion moments rather than errors.

The pizza with halves and fourths — cutting and sharing included — is free forever. Premium adds the chocolate bar with its molded squares, the sheet cake, thirds, sixths and eighths, six equivalence tray tasks where children prove that two fourths fill one half exactly, and eight sharing stories, all in eleven languages with grammatically correct spoken fraction names.
howToUse: Project the kitchen and pick a food — the pizza is free; the chocolate bar and cake are Premium.
Pick the pieces with the partition chips: halves, thirds, fourths, sixths, or eighths.
Have a child drag the knife along a guide line — a correct line cuts with a slice sound and the spoken fraction name; an off-center line shows its unequal pieces and heals.
Tap 'Share it', choose the number of friends, and drag one slice onto each plate — talk about leftovers and empty plates when they happen.
In Premium, open 'Fill the tray' to prove equivalence: two fourths fill one half exactly, and the tray glows honey-gold when the fit is perfect.
classroomIdeas: Predict-then-cut: before a child drags the knife, the class votes on which guide line will make equal pieces — then the cut settles it.
Fair-share circle time: cut fourths for four friends, then ask 'what if a fifth friend arrives?' and let the leftover discussion run.
Equal-or-not gallery: cut along the off-center line on purpose, let the unequal pieces sit, and have children describe WHY they are not fair shares.
Fraction-word echo: mute your own voice and have the class say the spoken fraction name together each time a cut lands.
Story problems: use the built-in sharing stories as warm-ups, then re-enact them with real snack-time sharing.
